clinicalPearls: Oral candidiasis is usually an opportunistic infection by Candida species, most often Candida albicans, and typically signals a local or systemic predisposing factor
The pseudomembranous form (thrush) shows white curd-like plaques that wipe off to reveal an erythematous, sometimes bleeding, base
Erythematous (atrophic) candidiasis presents as a red, sore mucosa or a depapillated tongue, and is common under dentures or after antibiotics
Angular cheilitis at the mouth corners frequently coexists and reflects candidal and bacterial colonisation with local moisture
Denture stomatitis appears as erythema confined to the denture-bearing palatal mucosa and relates to poor denture hygiene and continuous wear
Common predisposing factors include inhaled or systemic corticosteroids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, xerostomia, diabetes, and immunosuppression
Management combines antifungal therapy with correction of the underlying cause, including denture hygiene and control of dry mouth
Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis presents as an adherent white patch that will not rub off and carries a small malignant potential warranting biopsy
reference.pathophysiology: Candida species are common oral commensals kept in check by intact mucosal defences, salivary factors, and the resident microbiota. Disruption of this balance allows overgrowth and conversion to an invasive hyphal form that adheres to and penetrates the epithelium. Local factors such as denture coverage, dry mouth, and topical steroids, together with systemic factors such as antibiotics, immunosuppression, diabetes, and nutritional deficiency, create the conditions for opportunistic infection. The clinical pattern (pseudomembranous, erythematous, or hyperplastic) reflects the host state and chronicity rather than different organisms.
additionalDifferentials: Oral leukoplakia and other keratotic white lesions
Geographic tongue for the atrophic form
Mucosal manifestations of anaemia or nutritional deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Oral swab, smear, or oral rinse for microscopy and culture
Biopsy for adherent white patches to assess hyperplastic candidiasis and dysplasia
Blood glucose and screening for diabetes
Haematinics (iron, folate, B12) where atrophic or recurrent disease
Evaluation for immunodeficiency, including HIV, in unexplained or severe cases
redFlags: Unexplained or severe oral candidiasis in a previously healthy adult raising suspicion of undiagnosed HIV or other immunodeficiency
Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis with dysplasia and potential for malignant transformation
Extension into the oesophagus with dysphagia suggesting significant immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Most acute candidiasis responds well to antifungal treatment when predisposing factors are corrected, but recurrence is common if the underlying cause persists, and chronic hyperplastic lesions require monitoring for dysplasia.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent candidiasis without seeking and correcting the underlying predisposing factor
Assuming an adherent white patch is thrush when it is hyperplastic candidiasis or leukoplakia needing biopsy
Overlooking denture hygiene and continuous wear as the driver of denture stomatitis
Missing an immunocompromising condition in unexplained or florid infection
management: Give topical antifungals (nystatin suspension or miconazole oral gel) for localised disease, and a systemic azole (fluconazole) for extensive, refractory or immunocompromised cases
Correct local predisposing factors: rinse the mouth after inhaled corticosteroids, improve denture hygiene, remove dentures overnight, and manage xerostomia
Treat coexisting angular cheilitis with a topical antifungal, adding antibacterial cover where staphylococcal or streptococcal colonisation is present
Address systemic drivers by optimising glycaemic control in diabetes, correcting iron, folate and B12 deficiency, and reviewing broad-spectrum antibiotic and corticosteroid use
For denture stomatitis, disinfect the denture and apply antifungal to its fitting surface alongside hygiene measures
Biopsy chronic hyperplastic (adherent) plaques and monitor for dysplasia
Investigate for underlying immunodeficiency including HIV in unexplained, severe or recurrent disease and refer accordingly
